title: He set his face (Luke 9:51–62)
hook: he turns toward Jerusalem; foxes have holes, but he has nowhere to lay his head

segments.voice: Yesterday, John stopped a stranger from driving out demons, and a child was set beside Jesus while the disciples argued about rank. Your line was the least is the greatest. Whose need did you put first? Day five hundred thirty-eight.

Here, halfway through chapter nine, Luke's Gospel turns a corner, and you can almost feel the road tilt. In the King James words: "when the time was come that he should be received up, he stedfastly set his face to go to Jerusalem." From here on, Jesus is walking. The Good Samaritan, the prodigal son, Zacchaeus in the tree: Luke sets them on the road to Jerusalem, the city where Jesus has already said what is waiting. Set his face. Some readers hear an echo of the prophet Isaiah, where God's servant says: "therefore have I set my face like a flint." Flint. Hard stone. Not stubbornness. Resolve.

The road goes through Samaria first. In John's Gospel, a Samaritan woman names one old dispute between Samaritans and Jews: where the right place to worship is. Jesus sends messengers ahead to find a place to stay, and a Samaritan village turns them away, Luke says, because he was heading to Jerusalem. James and John are furious: "Lord, wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven, and consume them, even as Elias did?" Fire from heaven, like Elijah. And Luke says: "he turned, and rebuked them." They simply go to another village. Then three people meet him on the road. The first says, I'll follow you anywhere. Jesus answers: "Foxes have holes, and birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head." Anywhere includes nowhere. To the second, Jesus says: follow me. The man says, let me first go and bury my father. And Jesus says something startling: "Let the dead bury their dead." Readers differ on what it meant: some think the father had just died, others that the man meant to wait until his father died someday. The text doesn't say. What's clear is the urgency. The third says, let me first say goodbye to my family. And Jesus answers with a farmer's picture: "No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God." It's a plowman's picture: look back over your shoulder and the furrow goes crooked. You keep your eyes on a point ahead, and you walk toward it.
screen: `HAND TO THE PLOUGH, NO LOOKING BACK.`
then, large: `HE STEDFASTLY SET HIS FACE TO GO TO JERUSALEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set your face toward one hard thing. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind something you keep circling and not doing. A hard conversation. A doctor's appointment. A debt to face, an apology to make, a job application, a habit to end. Let one come up. Notice how you usually look back: the excuses, the let-me-first, the someday. Now picture a plowman with a point fixed on the far side of the field. Picture your face set toward your hard thing, calm, steady, flint, not angry. Choose the very first step, the one you could take today. If you pray, you can ask for a steady face. If you don't, simply fix your eyes on the step. The bell holds the time.
Flint, the hard stone Isaiah uses for an unbending resolve: Luke's turning point, where Jesus sets his face to go to Jerusalem and will not be turned back.
Your line: no looking back. Take the first step toward your hard thing today, and when the let-me-first voices start, keep your eyes on the point ahead. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Commentators call this long stretch of Luke the travel narrative, and some Christians read through it slowly, a few verses a day, as a journey toward Jerusalem and Holy Week.

original.note: Greek: he set firm his face. the King James Bible says stedfastly set his face.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus was being stubborn.
what it means: he chooses, calmly, to walk toward Jerusalem and what waits there, and asks his followers not to keep looking back.
what a scholar hears: some hear Isaiah 50:7 behind it, "have I set my face like a flint," and 9:51 opens what commentators call Luke's travel narrative.
